title: Strain-Induced Detuning of a Dressed Nitrogen-Vacancy Qubit: Effective Two-Level Theory and Its Validity
authors: Jihyeon Jeon, Donghun Lee, Seok-Kyun Son, Nojoon Myoung
abstract: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond can be operated as a microwave-dressed qubit. In the ideal two-level limit, its transition frequency is first-order insensitive to static magnetic fields, providing robustness against magnetic detuning noise. In practical diamond devices, however, residual transverse crystal strain mixes the $\ket{m_{s}=\pm1}$ spin sublevels and modifies the dressed qubit. In this study, we derive an analytical effective two-level model of a strained dressed NV qubit by perturbatively eliminating the far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed Hamiltonian. We obtain closed-form expressions for the dressed-state splitting, the spin-locking mixing angle, and the longitudinal magnetic-field coupling. We show that transverse strain shifts the dressed-state resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis. These two effects restore a finite DC-field response and thereby quantify the loss of magnetic robustness. We demonstrate these features in simulated pulsed electron spin resonance spectra that incorporate rate-equation-based optical readout. We further derive exact validity criteria from the eigenvalues and spectator weights of the full three-level Hamiltonian. For practical use, we reduce these criteria to two controlled guidelines: the spectator-like branch must remain above the nominal upper dressed state, and its branch-specific admixture must remain small. A validity diagram over the axial-field--transverse-strain plane summarizes these approximate conditions and provides practical guidelines for designing dressed-NV sensing experiments.
summary: This paper develops an effective two-level theory to model a dressed Nitrogen-Vacancy qubit, accounting for detrimental effects from residual transverse crystal strain. By perturbatively eliminating spectator states, the authors derive key parameters and quantify how strain degrades the qubit's inherent magnetic robustness. The work is vital for experimentalists needing reliable guidelines on when simplified models are valid for quantum sensing applications.
main_problem: The study quantifies how residual transverse crystal strain degrades the magnetic robustness of a dressed Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) qubit, which is crucial for reliable quantum sensing.
main_result: Strain shifts the dressed resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis, restoring a finite DC-field response that quantifies the loss of magnetic robustness. The paper also provides rigorous validity criteria for simplified models.
method: The authors derive an effective two-level model by perturbatively eliminating a far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed Hamiltonian using Löwdin–Feshbach partitioning.
model_or_system: The system is the NV center in diamond operated as a microwave-dressed qubit, modeled by a full three-level Hamiltonian ($H_{	ext{full}}$) that includes strain ($	ext{g}_{\perp}$) and an axial field ($	ext{B}_z$).
key_observables: Dressed-state splitting ($\Omega_D$), spin-locking mixing angle ($	heta$), longitudinal magnetic-field coupling ($m_q$), and simulated pulsed electron spin resonance (ESR) spectra.
important_parameters: Transverse strain ($	ext{g}_{\perp}$), axial magnetic field ($	ext{B}_z$), and the ratio of spectator state admixture to qubit splitting ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the system can be accurately reduced to an effective two-level model by neglecting coupling to a far-detuned spectator state, leading to derived validity guidelines.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic level structures showing strain effects on eigenfrequencies (full vs. reduced models) and present simulated pulsed-ESR spectra demonstrating the appearance of spectator transitions at low fields.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the effective two-level Hamiltonian via perturbation theory to obtaining closed-form expressions for key parameters, followed by rigorous derivation of validity criteria using exact eigenvalue analysis, culminating in practical guidelines summarized on a field/strain plane.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides necessary theoretical tools and operational boundaries (validity diagrams) for designing high-fidelity quantum sensing protocols using solid-state qubits like NV centers.
